name: Serving Engines and Continuous Batching
question: How many requests can one GPU serve, and at what cost?
summary: When you run open-weight models yourself, the serving engine decides how much work each GPU does. A naive server generates one request at a time and leaves the GPU mostly idle. Static batching waits for a batch to fill and for its longest answer to finish. Engines such as vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and TGI use continuous batching, which adds a new request to the running batch at every decoding step, and paged KV-cache memory (PagedAttention), which packs many more sequences into GPU memory. The result is several times more tokens per second per GPU and a lower cost per million tokens. Capacity is then sized from load and a latency target. Prefix caching, speculative decoding and disaggregated prefill are separate techniques in this module that these engines also implement.
useCases: Self-hosting open models for cost, data residency or latency
Serving a fine-tuned or distilled small model
High-volume internal workloads such as classification or extraction

steps.title: Start a continuous-batching server
steps.text: Bharat Bol, a fictional voice-bot company, serves an 8B model with vLLM. The server exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so the app code does not change.

steps.title: Let the batch grow
steps.text: max-num-seqs lets up to 128 sequences share the GPU. New requests join the running batch at each step instead of waiting for a batch to finish.

steps.title: Leave room for the KV cache
steps.text: 90% of GPU memory is given to weights and the paged KV cache. A shorter max context of 8,192 tokens leaves room for more sequences.

steps.title: Load-test at real traffic
steps.text: Replay 8 requests a second of real prompts for two minutes. One-at-a-time tests make any GPU look slow.

steps.title: Read p95 and throughput
steps.text: One GPU serves the 2,400 tokens a second but runs 80% busy, so p95 is 18 s. Two GPUs bring p95 to 8 s.

steps.title: Compare the cost
steps.text: At ₹220 per GPU-hour, two GPUs cost about ₹51 per million output tokens. Compare that, and p95, with a hosted API before committing.

practice.scenario: Bharat Bol, a fictional voice-bot company, self-hosts an 8B model for Hindi support calls because call transcripts must stay in its own cloud. Its first server generated one answer at a time and queued at 2 requests a second. With vLLM’s continuous batching and paged KV cache, one GPU handles 8 requests a second (2,400 output tokens a second) at 80% busy with a p95 of 18 s; two GPUs bring p95 to 8 s at about ₹51 per million output tokens.

industries.use: Hindi and regional-language voice bots with data kept in-country
Internal document extraction on self-hosted models
High-volume product tagging with a small fine-tuned model

practice.analogy: A restaurant kitchen that starts the next order on any free burner the moment a dish is done, instead of cooking tables in fixed rounds and waiting for the slowest dish.

library.name: vLLM
library.what: A high-throughput serving engine with continuous batching, PagedAttention and an OpenAI-compatible server.

practice.note: Needs a CUDA GPU with enough memory for the model. The offline API shown batches all prompts at once; for live traffic use vllm serve and a load test.

samples.code:
import time
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

llm = LLM(model="Qwen/Qwen3-8B", gpu_memory_utilization=0.90, max_model_len=8192)
params = SamplingParams(max_tokens=300, temperature=0.2)

prompts = [f"Summarise this support call in Hindi, ticket {i}: ..." for i in range(512)]
t = time.perf_counter()
outs = llm.generate(prompts, params)
secs = time.perf_counter() - t

tokens = sum(len(o.outputs[0].token_ids) for o in outs)
print(f"{tokens / secs:.0f} output tokens/s across {len(prompts)} prompts")

numericDrill.question: Two GPUs at ₹220 an hour each serve 2,400 output tokens a second. What is the cost per million output tokens in ₹?
numericDrill.answer: Tokens an hour: 2,400 × 3,600 = 86,40,000 = 8.64 million. Cost an hour: ₹440. ₹440 ÷ 8.64 ≈ ₹50.9 per million tokens.

interview.question: What is continuous batching?
interview.answer: The server adds new requests to the running batch at every decoding step and removes finished ones, instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish. GPUs stay busy, so throughput rises several-fold.

interview.question: Why does p95 latency jump near full utilisation?
interview.answer: As load approaches capacity, requests queue; waiting time grows sharply above about 80% busy. Size capacity so peak load leaves headroom.
